title: Sell Mineral Rights in Tyler County, WV
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Tyler County, WV
metaDescription: Tyler County minerals span Sistersville's historic oil-boom deed record and modern Marcellus/Utica horizontal units — deep courthouse title work either way.
heroLead: Tyler County carries two eras of oil and gas history in one deed book — Sistersville's 1890s boomtown oil rush and today's Marcellus and Utica horizontal development.
intro: Sistersville was, for a stretch in the 1890s, one of the busiest oil boomtowns in the country, with derricks packed along the Ohio River and enough drilling activity that the town briefly rivaled far larger cities for oil-money wealth. That history left Tyler County with an extraordinarily dense early deed record — severances, leases, and assignments recorded decades before anyone thought about horizontal Marcellus wells.

Modern development picked the county back up as core Marcellus and Utica/Point Pleasant acreage, with operators running horizontal units across Middlebourne, Paden City, and the rural acreage between them. The result is a county where a single mineral interest can carry both a 19th-century oil lease history and a 21st-century horizontal unit obligation, and both matter for figuring out what it's actually worth.

sections.heading: Sistersville's boomtown deed record
paragraphs: The volume of oil-era transactions recorded around Sistersville in the 1890s and early 1900s means the Tyler County Courthouse in Middlebourne holds an unusually thick set of deed and lease books for a county this size. Tracing a mineral interest back to its original severance often means working through several of these older volumes, since tracts were frequently subdivided, re-leased, and partially assigned multiple times during the boom years.

That density is a double-edged sword: it means the records exist, but it also means more opportunities for a break in the chain — an unrecorded assignment, a missed probate — that a proper title review needs to catch before a sale.

sections.heading: Modern Marcellus and Utica/Point Pleasant units
paragraphs: Tyler County sits in core stacked-pay territory, with operators developing both the Marcellus and the deeper Utica/Point Pleasant in parts of the county, similar to the pattern in neighboring Marshall County. Horizontal units here tend to be large and long-lateral, pooling acreage from multiple original farm tracts into a single spacing unit.

For owners whose interest traces back to a Sistersville-era severance, confirming how that historic interest maps onto a modern unit plat is essential — the unit boundaries were drawn using current surveys, not the metes-and-bounds descriptions common in 1890s deeds, so the two records don't always translate cleanly without a professional check.

sections.heading: Heirship across more than a century of Tyler County ownership
paragraphs: Between the oil-boom era severances and the generations since, Tyler County mineral interests frequently carry heir counts in the dozens, with descendants scattered well outside the county. Paden City and the rural acreage around Middlebourne both show this pattern regularly — small fractional shares, some producing under legacy leases, some sitting under newer Marcellus units, almost all needing an heirship affidavit or probate step before a clean sale can close.
We buy fractional interests directly from individual Tyler County heirs, whether the underlying interest traces to a 1890s Sistersville lease or a recent horizontal unit.

sections.heading: Confirming the operator of record before valuing an interest
paragraphs: Tyler County acreage has changed operator hands multiple times over the past fifteen years as companies have bought, sold, and consolidated positions across the play, and it's common for a mineral owner's records to lag behind the current reality. Before valuing any Tyler County interest, confirming which company currently operates the well or unit — and whether current royalty payments reflect their terms rather than a predecessor's — is a necessary step, not an optional one.

This is especially true for interests tracing to Sistersville-era leases, where the original lessee company may have dissolved, merged, or sold its position more than once since the lease was first signed.

faqs.question: Why is Tyler County's deed record so much older and denser than nearby counties?
faqs.answer: Sistersville's 1890s oil boom generated an unusually high volume of leases, severances, and assignments in a short period, all recorded at the Tyler County Courthouse. That density means more historical records to trace, and more chances for a gap in the chain.

faqs.question: Is my interest under both the Marcellus and the Utica/Point Pleasant?
faqs.answer: Possibly — Tyler County has areas of stacked-pay development similar to Marshall County. Checking your unit plat and any division orders against both formations confirms whether you have one royalty stream or two.

faqs.question: How does an 1890s deed description map onto a modern horizontal unit?
faqs.answer: Not automatically. Old metes-and-bounds descriptions from the boom era don't always align cleanly with modern unit plats drawn from current surveys, which is why a title professional needs to confirm the overlap before valuing the interest.

faqs.question: My great-grandfather's Sistersville-era lease is still listed as the governing lease — is that normal?
faqs.answer: It can be, if the lease is still held by production and was never released. It's worth confirming the lease is still in force and that royalty payments (not an old flat rate) are actually being made under current terms.

faqs.question: Does a Tyler County interest need separate title work for its oil-era and Marcellus-era history?
faqs.answer: A single title review typically covers both, tracing the full chain from the original 1890s severance through any modern lease and unit assignments affecting the same tract.
